    Four reinforcing loops

    Affinity to consume healthy food depends on category consideration, product utility (attribute states weighted by each segment's sensitivity) and the built food environment. Four reinforcing loops close back on consumption: R1 socio-behavioural, R2 marketing, R3 product, R4 built environment. Highlighted tags show the interventions in your current scenario.

    Who can intervene, and where

    Full analysis of the corrected Struben model. All charts and tables on this page are computed live by the same model that runs the simulator. A print-ready PDF version is in Downloads.

    Executive summary

    Healthy-food markets do not move because a single actor pushes. They move when the market infrastructure, the slowly accumulating capabilities, consumer consideration and food-environment institutions behind every purchase, changes in step. Struben's model formalizes this as four reinforcing feedback loops acting on two consumer segments whose infrastructure is unequal from the start.

    Five conclusions for the industry

    1. Isolated interventions underdeliver. Education campaigns fade once they stop; price policy and accessibility help but plateau. Each pushes one loop while the others pull back toward the old equilibrium.
    2. Innovation direction decides who benefits. High-end (taste-led) innovation raises utility for affluent consumers and lowers it for price-sensitive ones, widening the gap. Affordable (cost-led) innovation narrows it slightly but barely scales.
    3. Directed technical change scales the market and pulls in private R&D, but the low-SES segment lags without demand-side and access support.
    4. Convergent innovation is the only package that delivers scale, equity and firm investment together. Directed innovation, consumer education and accessibility programs reinforce each other because they act on all four loops at once.
    5. Firms are part of the feedback, not bystanders. Budgets follow perceived returns: subsidized innovation partly crowds out own R&D, while improved returns pull it in. Strategy should be designed with these responses in mind.
    How to read the numbers. This is a stylized, behavioral model calibrated to Struben's published trajectories. It ranks pathways and reveals behavior modes (fade, lock-in, tipping); it is not a sales forecast. Section 8 shows which conclusions survive ±30% changes in every key assumption.

    2. Context: why healthy food is a market-transformation problem

    Struben places healthy food among sustainability-oriented markets (recycling, rooftop solar, plant-based meat, sustainable fashion) that must transform an existing market rather than create a new one. Progress is slow and failure-prone: fast fashion keeps growing despite circularity rhetoric; Better Place burned close to one billion dollars before it could build battery-swapping infrastructure.

    His typology of market formation (Struben & Lee, 2024) sorts markets by demand and supply challenges. Where infrastructure exists (Groupon), there is no collective-action problem. Where it is clear what must be built (mobile payments, online streaming), free-riding is the risk. Where it is unclear (microbrewing, minivans), the start-up problem dominates. With large demand and supply challenges (organic food, edible insects, grass-fed meat), coordination across actors becomes essential. Equitable healthy food sits in that last quadrant.

    Evidence Struben cited (North America)

    ~13.5 million US residents have limited access to supermarkets
    46.5% of low-income households are food insecure; 78% of these live in food deserts
    Nearest grocery store: 2.1 miles in food deserts vs 0.5 miles elsewhere
    25% higher type 2 diabetes risk; children 2.2× more likely to have iron-deficiency anemia
    Food-desert households spend a larger budget share on food, ~30% of it on processed foods
    Estimated US$6.5 billion per year in lost productivity from diet-related illness
    Well-intended efforts exist (NYC FRESH: 150,000 residents gained store access; 16 large food companies cut calories sold by 10.6% in 2007–2012), yet gaps persist

    Struben's sources include worldmetrics.org compilations, Frederick, Snellman & Putnam (2013), Ng, Slining & Popkin (2014), Nakamura et al. (2014). Several are secondary compilations and should be re-verified before external citation.

    Why it matters now for food and beverage companies in Mexico

    MX$3.08 / LIEPS on sugar-sweetened beverages from 1 Jan 2026, up about 87% from MX$1.64; light/zero drinks taxed at MX$1.50 / L for the first time.
    75.2%Adult overweight and obesity prevalence in ENSANUT 2018 (71.3% in 2012); diabetes rose from 9.2% to 10.3% of adults.
    Oct 2020NOM-051 front-of-pack warning labels in force; also restricts school sale and marketing of products carrying warnings.

    In the model's language, the tax and labels act on price and consideration (1b, 1a), while industry reformulation, such as the announced 30% calorie reduction in some Mexican soft-drink packs, acts on capabilities and attribute states (R3). The model's central warning applies directly: policy pushes on one loop will fade or concentrate benefits unless capabilities, consideration and access in lower-income channels (tienditas, school food, traditional trade) move together.

    3. The model: four reinforcing loops

    R1 Socio-behavioural influence

    Consumption raises social pressure and habituation, which builds category consideration, which raises affinity and consumption. Learning from peers and social media is central; in the live poll, social media (19), other (18), mainstream media (15) and friends/family (15) dominated, versus 5 for "where I buy my food".

    R2 Marketing factors

    Consumption drives firm reinvestment and resources to the category; part becomes marketing spending, which builds consideration. Marketing is a flow: its effect lasts only as long as spending continues.

    R3 Product factors

    Firm resources fund R&D, which builds industry capabilities; capabilities improve attribute states (price, taste, variety, nutrition); weighted by attribute sensitivity, they raise product utility and affinity. Capabilities are a stock that obsolesces slowly.

    R4 Built food environment

    Consumption and better attributes attract distribution networks, corner stores, school lunches and food services; accessibility raises affinity. In low-SES areas this stock starts lower and is funded more by public sources.

    The same loops explain both growth and lock-in. Run in reverse, they keep the low-SES segment's consideration, access and product fit low, which keeps consumption low. That is why the baseline is an equilibrium with a persistent gap.

    4. Formulation

    Key equations (Vensim notation, segment p ∈ {High-SES, Low-SES})

    HF Share[p] = Affinity HF[p] / (Affinity HF[p] + Affinity LH[p]) (logit choice) Affinity HF[p] = Base[p] · (Consideration[p]/C0[p])^1.85 · (Accessibility[p]/A0[p])^0.45 · EXP(Utility[p]) Utility[p] = TasteSens[p]·LN(Taste state) + PriceSens[p]·LN(Price state) (TasteSens .80/.56, PriceSens .46/1.0) Consideration[p] = INTEG((1−C)·(background + 0.1·Share + 0.95·marketing per capita + education) − C/7) Taste capability = INTEG(R&D productivity·(Firm R&D·0.5 + high-end funds) − capability/8) Taste state = (TasteCap/TC0)^0.3 · (CostCap/CC0)^−0.22 ; Price state = (CostCap/CC0)^0.3 · (TasteCap/TC0)^−0.3 · (1+subsidy) Accessibility[p] = INTEG((MIN(1, Share·(Taste·Price)^0.5) − A)/10 + public access programs[p]) Desired R&D intensity = 0.155 · (R&D productivity)^0.6 ; Desired marketing intensity = 0.21 · ((1−C̄0)/(1−C̄))^−0.3 R&D share, budget intensity = INTEG((desired − current)/5) ; Firm R&D = intensity·share·perceived revenue − 0.5·external funds

    All initial values are computed so that 2020 is an exact equilibrium matching Struben's baseline. Background exposure is backed out from the equilibrium condition, representing public and other sources of consideration.

    Firm behavior: three responses that matter

    • Returns pull. When R&D becomes more productive (directed technical change), the desired R&D budget rises, with a five-year adjustment.
    • Marketing saturation. When public programs raise consideration, the marketing budget firms need falls modestly.
    • Crowding out. Half of any external innovation funding is subtracted from firms' own R&D during the program (Struben's slides show this dip).

    5. Calibration and validation

    Baseline levels come directly from Struben's slides. Twenty-two behavioral parameters were then estimated by random-search calibration against 26 points read from his scenario charts, holding the model at equilibrium in 2020. The Vensim, Excel and HTML implementations were cross-checked: PySD (Vensim) and JS agree to machine precision, Excel to five decimals.

    ScenarioVariableYearStruben (chart)ModelΔ

    Good agreement on direction and magnitude for 2042 outcomes. The main residuals: the model under-predicts the late rise of high-SES share after high-end and affordable innovation, and reaches the directed-change R&D peak at the end of the program (2027) rather than two years after (2029).

    Structural validity checks

    • Equilibrium test: with no interventions all stocks remain at 2020 values through 2042.
    • Extreme conditions: shares remain in [0,1]; zero R&D drives capabilities toward zero with an 8-year lifetime; access is capped at 1.
    • Feedback-loop tests: Struben reports that disabling feedbacks changes results materially; Section 8 repeats this for each loop.

    7. Impact comparison

    Struben evaluates interventions on three impacts: healthy-food scale, the equity gap, and healthy-food R&D efforts. The table adds persistence and the low-SES share reached.

    ScenarioScale 2042Equity gap 2042Firm R&D 2022–42Low-SES share 2042Reading
    Struben's reported figures for convergent innovation: scale +39%, equity gap −45%, R&D efforts +40%; adding high-end innovation narrows the gap less (−23%) but low-SES consumers still consume more healthy food than without it. This reconstruction reproduces the ranking and the trade-off (convergent +28% / −37% / +53%; adding high-end reduces gap closure to −28%), with smaller scale because metrics and parameters differ.

    8. Sensitivity analysis

    Each structural parameter was varied ±30% and the convergent and directed-change scenarios re-run against a re-run baseline. Bars show the range of the convergent scenario's scale effect; the table reports whether convergent innovation remains the best on scale and equity.

    TestConvergent scaleConvergent gapConvergent still beats 1a, 1b, 2a, 2b and 3 on scale and equity?

    Loop knock-out tests

    Loop disabledConvergent scaleConvergent gapInterpretation

    Knock-outs set the loop's link to zero (R1: social influence; R2: marketing effectiveness and budget response; R3: capability effect on attributes; R4: accessibility elasticity), with the baseline re-equilibrated each time.

    Finding to flag. In this reconstruction, accessibility programs alone (1c) close much of the gap. Struben did not report this run, and the result depends heavily on the accessibility elasticity and program strength calibrated within the convergent scenario. Treat it as a hypothesis to test with local data: if true, physical access in low-income channels is the binding constraint.

    9. Implications for food and beverage companies

    The model turns a public-health debate into an operating question: which stocks does my strategy build, for whom, and what happens when the program money stops?

    Loop / stockCompany leversLeading indicators to track
    R3 Industry capabilitiesDirect R&D at cost and taste together, not taste alone; reformulation (sugar, sodium) with sensory parity; shared standards and supplier development; co-funded R&D consortia.Cost per serving of healthy SKUs vs regular; sensory parity scores; share of R&D on value-tier healthy products.
    R1/R2 Category considerationCategory-building with public partners in low-income segments; sampling and habit formation (schools, workplaces); social-media and community influencers; consistent labeling communication.Trial and repeat rates by socioeconomic level; awareness and consideration tracking; earned versus paid exposure.
    R4 Systems & institutionsRoute-to-market for healthy SKUs in traditional trade (tienditas), refrigeration and assortment programs, food service and school channels, municipal partnerships.Numeric distribution of healthy SKUs by channel and neighborhood income; out-of-stocks; cooler coverage.
    Firm budget decisionsAvoid letting subsidies replace own R&D; set budget rules on long-run returns, not campaign-period sales; ring-fence healthy-portfolio R&D through program end.Own R&D vs external funds; marketing-to-R&D ratio in the healthy portfolio.

    Decision rules from the model

    1. Pair every innovation with an access plan for price-sensitive segments. Otherwise, success widens the gap and invites regulation.
    2. Treat campaigns as sustained investments or pair them with infrastructure. Consideration decays with a multi-year memory; temporary campaigns fade.
    3. Join or convene cross-sector coalitions (government, retailers, NGOs, suppliers). The convergent package outperforms the sum of its parts.
    4. Plan for delays. Capabilities and access take 5–10 years to build; judge programs on 2030+ trajectories, not first-year sales.

    Making it company-specific

    Replace stylized segments with company data: sell-out by channel and neighborhood income (e.g. retail-link data), price elasticities by segment, distribution and cooler census, consumer tracking. Re-estimate the elasticities, then use the simulator to test portfolio, pricing and route-to-market plans against the 2026 IEPS and labeling environment.

    10. Limitations

    • Stylized structure. Two segments, two categories, one aggregate firm (Struben uses two firm types); attributes condensed to taste and cost capabilities.
    • Reconstructed parameters. Calibrated to chart readings, not the authors' parameter file; levels are approximate.
    • Exogenous context held fixed. Income, culture, residential mobility and agricultural supply do not change endogenously, as Struben noted in the Q&A.
    • No health module. Consumption shares do not feed back into health outcomes or productivity.
    • Data sources. Some statistics on the original slides come from secondary compilations; verify before external citation.

    How to use Food-ROADS

    Every slider starts at status quo. Move a slider to add an intervention; the colored bar on its left marks what you changed. Click ⋯ for what the lever does and which loop it acts on.

    Read the two graphs. Choose any output in each graph's title menu. The thin gray line is the baseline; the bold lines are your scenario. Hover or touch a graph to read values. The shaded band is the intervention period.

    Watch the headline. The yellow number is the low-SES healthy-food share in 2042, the model's equivalent of En-ROADS' temperature: the outcome that tells you whether the market is transforming for everyone.

    Try the scenarios menu for Struben's experiments, then build your own combination. A pathway is convincing when it raises scale, closes the gap, and keeps firms investing after the program ends.

    Assumptions (last column) let you stress-test structure. Conclusions worth presenting should survive reasonable changes.

    Report holds the full analysis; Downloads has the Vensim, Excel, PDF and deck versions plus CSV exports.

    Stylized model for strategic discussion, not a forecast. Look and feel inspired by En-ROADS (Climate Interactive and MIT Sloan); this tool is not affiliated with them.
